strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful computer-vision problem: automatically discovering reusable visual interventions for LVLM perception failures. Under Algorithms/General, separating high-level ideas from executable implementations and propagating qualitative experimental feedback constitutes a coherent methodological contribution.

The held-out results are promising. Across nine tasks, SEVEX improves average accuracy from 71.6% to 78.9%, with particularly substantial gains on LineIntersections (73.0% to 90.5%) and Jigsaw (75.8% to 95.8%). These gains use only 30 development examples per task.

Task-wise prompt reuse offers practical value. Table 2 reports inference token consumption close to naive inference and substantially below SketchPad. The paper also explicitly accounts for upfront exploration tokens.

The qualitative examples make the approach concrete, particularly repurposing depth estimation to assess completed jigsaw images. Component ablations averaged over five runs provide preliminary support for the design, while tool descriptions, hyperparameters, development indices, and several agent prompts aid reproducibility.
weaknesses: The comparisons do not adequately isolate the proposed search algorithm from the benefits of task-wise optimization and reusable programs. SketchPad generates programs per sample, while SketchPad+APE optimizes its textual instructions. A budget-matched baseline that directly searches reusable visual programs, plus random or standard UCT search over the same idea space, is needed to establish the incremental value of SEVEX and novelty-guided selection.

The central non-transferability claim is contradicted by substantial evidence in Table 4. The Gemini-discovered prompt improves all three models and achieves 59.1% on GPT-4o, exceeding the GPT-discovered prompt's 57.1%. The Claude-discovered prompt also improves every model over naive inference. These results demonstrate model-dependent rankings and occasional negative transfer, but do not establish that prompts rarely transfer or that independent discovery is necessary for every model.

Evidence for exploration stability and individual components is limited. Figure 5 covers only two tasks, reports development accuracy without uncertainty, and does not separately ablate novelty and saturation. Main-table run aggregation is unclear, and no held-out variability or repeated development splits are reported. A smaller development-to-test gap alone does not establish search stability.

Important implementation details remain unresolved. Equation (2) divides by the number of executed children, which is zero for a newly expanded parent, without specifying an initialization convention. Score normalization and rescaling are unspecified. Appendix A's 'Implementation prompt' actually requests an idea and excludes code, duplicating the idea-generation prompt rather than documenting the engineer stage. These omissions materially hinder faithful reproduction.

The efficiency evidence supports token savings, but not complete computational savings. Token counts omit detection, segmentation, and depth-estimation execution costs, which are especially relevant to the highlighted Jigsaw strategy. Runtime or monetary accounting that includes external tools would strengthen the practical efficiency claim.

The source of the accuracy improvements is insufficiently separated. SEVEX jointly changes textual instructions, few-shot examples, image transformations, and external-model use; Figure 6's successful Gemini strategy is few-shot prompting. Text-only optimization and simple fixed-tool controls would clarify how much improvement specifically requires discovered visual manipulation. Overall, the promising results make this a close decision, but the missing controlled comparisons and overstated central conclusion leave a slight preference for rejection.

The statistical and generalization evidence is limited. Search repeatedly uses only 30 development images per task, while the main test results lack reported uncertainty and a clear account of repeated search runs. Some gains are small, and SubwayMap falls from 80.0% development accuracy to 62.8% test accuracy. The reported generalization gaps alone do not establish stability, particularly when comparing methods with very different development performance.

The claimed 273-inference break-even point divides exploration cost by SketchPad's inference cost without subtracting SEVEX's ongoing inference cost; the reported averages imply approximately 300 inferences instead. Table 2 also contains inconsistent SketchPad benchmark-average token costs. These accounting issues are correctable, but the broader efficiency claim requires measured runtime or monetary costs.
